content: Medical education refers to the training and education required to become a medical practitioner. This includes both the initial training to qualify as a doctor and any further training undertaken afterward, such as during residency. The structure and content of medical education and training vary significantly across different countries. Various teaching methods are employed in medical education, and this field remains an active area of research in educational methodologies. Entry-level medical education programs are tertiary-level courses offered at medical schools. Depending on the country and institution, these programs may either admit students directly after high school (undergraduate-entry programs, common in Europe, India, and China) or require a prior degree (graduate-entry programs, typical in the United States). The initial phase of medical education is traditionally divided into preclinical and clinical studies. Preclinical studies focus on foundational sciences such as anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, pharmacology, and pathology. Clinical studies, on the other hand, involve training in various medical specialties, including internal medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, psychiatry, and surgery. However, many medical schools now adopt systems-based curricula, which integrate learning across disciplines. Additionally, there has been an increase in dual-degree programs, such as MD-PhD (combining medical training with research) and MD-MBA (combining medical training with management education), though these programs have faced criticism. After completing entry-level medical education, newly graduated doctors are typically required to undergo a period of supervised practice before they are granted full registration. This period, often lasting one year, is commonly referred to as an internship, provisional registration, or residency. Further specialized training in a specific field of medicine may follow. In some countries, specialization begins immediately after completing entry-level training, while in others, junior doctors are required to complete several years of generalist training before pursuing specialization. Examples of medical education systems include those in Australia, the United Kingdom, the United States, India, Hong Kong, and the Philippines. Each system has its own unique structure and approach to training medical professionals.
